lead: This essay does not treat the Gospel of John as a document in which a human author deliberately constructed a modern philosophical argument. It proceeds from the confessional premise that Scripture was written through human authors under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and it follows the connections, repetitions, and patterns of witness found in the text as they are examined and interpreted by a present-day reader.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 The Question

The central question raised by the Gospel of John is not limited to whether Yeshua is the Messiah. A more fundamental question is whether Israel could recognize the God whom they sought and worshiped through Scripture when He actually appeared among them as a human being.

As the narrative of John unfolds, the answer is paradoxical. Israel possessed the writings of Moses and the prophets, studied the word of God, and sought God. Yet when that very God revealed Himself in human flesh, many judged Him to be merely a man. Unbelief therefore cannot be explained only by a lack of evidence. It also involved an inability to accept that God could reveal Himself in human form.

This essay follows that movement in four directions. It examines Yeshua's declaration that Moses and the Scriptures testify about Him, the way the glory and authority that belong to the God of Israel are connected to Yeshua, the relationship between His words and His signs, and the way His real humanity and death on the cross became decisive stumbling blocks. It then considers how the resurrection overturns the human judgment made at the cross.
Chapter 2 The Declaration "Moses Wrote About Me"

In John 5:39, Yeshua tells those who search the Scriptures that the Scriptures testify about Him. In John 5:46, He goes further and says that Moses wrote about Him. If this statement is limited to a few predictions in the Torah about a future Messiah, it becomes difficult to account for the broader pattern that runs through the Gospel of John.

There are, of course, direct anticipations of a future figure, such as the passage in Deuteronomy 18. For that reason, not every line written by Moses should be mechanically turned into a direct prediction of a future person named Yeshua. At the same time, the Torah is not merely a list of messianic predictions. Its central subject is YHWH, the God who delivered Israel from Egypt, spoke at Sinai, established the covenant, gave the commandments, and dwelt among His people in the tabernacle.

This raises a larger question about the relationship between the divine revelation recorded by Moses and Yeshua. The Gospel of John does not separate Yeshua from the God whom Moses wrote about as though they were unrelated realities. Instead, John repeatedly connects Yeshua with language, glory, works, and authority that belonged to God in Exodus and Isaiah.

In this sense, the declaration "Moses wrote about Me" can be understood as more than the fulfillment of isolated predictions. The salvation and presence of God to which the Torah bears witness reach their fullest manifestation in Yeshua.
Chapter 3 The God of Torah and the Word Made Flesh
In the beginning was the Word. The Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

The crucial point is that John does not say merely that a word belonging to God was delivered to a human being. The word of God came to the prophets, but in the case of Yeshua, the Word became flesh. The incarnation therefore cannot be adequately described as God choosing a human being to act as His representative. The opening of John connects the very existence of Yeshua within human history with God's self-revelation.

The statement in John 1:14 that the Word "dwelt among us" is also important. The expression carries the sense of pitching a tent or dwelling in a tabernacle. In Exodus, the glory of God filled the tabernacle. In John, the language of divine presence is concentrated in the Word who became flesh.

In the past, the tabernacle stood among Israel and the glory of God dwelt there. John now says of the Word made flesh, "We have seen His glory." The God who dwelt in the tabernacle and Yeshua, the Word made flesh, should therefore not be treated as two unrelated revelations. They can be understood as the presence of the same God manifested in a new way.
Chapter 4 "Before Abraham Was Born, I Am"

John 8:58 presents this connection with exceptional force. Yeshua declares, "Before Abraham was born, I am." In terms of human birth, Yeshua appeared in history long after Abraham. To those standing before Him, He looked like a man who was not yet fifty years old. That is why they asked how He could have seen Abraham.

Yeshua does not answer by saying that He was created before Abraham. He says, "Before Abraham was born, I am." The subject of the statement is the very Yeshua who is standing before them. He does not say that someone inside Him existed before Abraham.

This does not mean that His present physical body had existed materially before Abraham. John 1:14 says that the preexistent Word became flesh within history. The central point is that there is no personal break between the One who existed before Abraham and the One who now stands before them as a man.

His visible human birth took place in history, but the existence of the One speaking through that humanity reaches back before Abraham. A view of Yeshua as merely a specially chosen human being therefore does not fully account for the force of this self-declaration.
Chapter 5 "Whoever Has Seen Me Has Seen the Father"

In John 14, Philip asks Yeshua to show them the Father. Yeshua answers, "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father." This is one of the clearest passages for understanding the meaning of the incarnation.

If Yeshua were only a prophet, a natural answer would be that He would show them the Father or teach them the way to the Father. Instead, He directly connects seeing Himself with seeing the Father. At the same time, He says that He is in the Father and that the Father is in Him.

Two facts stand together in this passage. Yeshua and the Father cannot be divided into two independent Gods, yet the relational language of Father and Son is not erased. The Father sends, the Son is sent, the Son prays to the Father, and the Son speaks of returning to the Father.

Taken as a whole, the Gospel of John can therefore be read as presenting the Father and the Son as relationally distinct without presenting them as two separate Gods. The central claim is that the invisible God reveals Himself in the incarnate Yeshua.
Chapter 6 God Appearing in Human Form and the Prohibition of Images

For Israel, such a claim was extremely difficult to accept. The Torah strictly forbids making an image of God for worship. Deuteronomy 4 grounds this prohibition in the fact that Israel saw no form of God at Sinai. They were not to make a human or animal image as a representation of Him. The premise is clear. God cannot be reduced to an image manufactured by human beings.

Idolatrous image-making and the incarnation, however, move in opposite directions. An idol is a human attempt to give God a form according to human imagination. The incarnation is God making Himself known to human beings. The first is a human construction. The second is divine self-revelation.

The Torah's prohibition of images and the incarnation in John should therefore not be treated as the same kind of event. Human beings are forbidden to fashion God according to their own design. That prohibition does not by itself establish that God is incapable of revealing Himself among human beings in a form He freely chooses.

At this point we can understand something of the shock experienced by many Jews of that time. The God they knew was the holy God who shook Sinai, descended in fire and cloud, and inspired fear even at the thought of drawing near. Yet a man from Galilee stood before them using language of an absolute kind that belonged to that God. The problem was not that there was no evidence. The person performing the signs looked radically different from what they expected God to look like.
Chapter 7 "You, a Man, Make Yourself God"

John 10:33 captures the judgment of the religious leaders with remarkable precision. Their charge was essentially this. "You are a man, yet You make Yourself God." This is where the conflict in John becomes especially clear.

The leaders looked at the movement in one direction. A man was claiming to be God. The Gospel of John presents the movement in the opposite direction. God became flesh and came among human beings. Two radically different judgments arise from looking at the same Yeshua.

Their unbelief therefore should not be reduced to malice or ignorance alone. The Yeshua standing before them was visibly human. He ate, walked, became tired, and had grown up in a known region. In John 6, people appeal to their knowledge of His family and ask how He can say that He came down from heaven.
Because they knew His human origin, they failed to recognize His true origin. They believed they knew where He came from, and precisely for that reason they did not know where He truly came from.
Chapter 8 The Signs as Evidence Pointing to Yeshua's Identity

Yeshua does not demand that people believe His claims without grounds. In John 5:36, He says that the works He does testify that the Father has sent Him. In John 10:37-38, He tells His hearers that even if they do not believe Him, they should consider the works.

The signs in John are therefore more than supernatural events. They function as evidence by which Yeshua's identity is to be judged. He turns water into wine, restores the sick, feeds a multitude, walks on the sea, gives sight to a man blind from birth, and calls Lazarus out of the tomb.

John places these signs beside Yeshua's self-declarations. He gives life and does not merely say that God gives life. He declares, "I am the resurrection and the life." He brings light and does not merely say that God is light. He declares, "I am the light of the world." When He speaks of protecting the sheep, He identifies Himself as the good shepherd.

A repeated pattern appears. His works testify to His words, and His words interpret the meaning of His works. Yet John 12 explains that many still did not believe even after seeing many signs, and it invokes Isaiah to describe a condition of judicial hardness. Unbelief is therefore not simply a lack of information. It is the refusal to acknowledge the One to whom the signs point.
Chapter 9 The Glory Isaiah Saw and the Glory of Yeshua

John 12:41 intensifies this connection. After quoting Isaiah 6, John says that Isaiah saw His glory and spoke about Him. In Isaiah 6, the prophet sees the glory of the Lord seated on the throne, and the passage centers on the Holy One of Israel.

John connects that glory to the context of unbelief in Yeshua. Yeshua therefore does not appear merely as a future human Messiah predicted by Isaiah. The glory of God seen by Isaiah is directly connected with the glory revealed in Yeshua.

This also matters when we read the statement "Moses wrote about Me." There is no need to turn every YHWH passage in Moses or Isaiah into a mechanical direct statement about Yeshua. Yet one of the striking features of John is that language of glory and divine existence that belonged to God in the Hebrew Scriptures is applied to Yeshua.

The interpretation advanced in this essay therefore does not stop with the claim that Yeshua is the predicted Messiah. It moves toward the claim that in this Messiah the God of Israel revealed His own glory.
Chapter 10 Why Yeshua Told the Samaritan Woman, "I Am He"

The account of the Samaritan woman in John 4 provides an important contrast. She says that the Messiah is coming and that He will explain all things. Yeshua answers her directly, "I who speak to you am He."

This does not mean that Yeshua concealed His identity from every Jew. His identity is disclosed throughout John in many ways. The declaration to the Samaritan woman is simply unusually direct. In disputes with religious leaders, by contrast, the more Yeshua explains His identity, the sharper the conflict becomes.

The reason is that the issue was larger than the title Messiah. What many could not accept was not only a claim about who the expected Messiah would be. The deeper claim was that the God they worshiped was revealing Himself in this human being.

The Samaritan woman accepted Yeshua's words despite the limits of her knowledge, and many people came to Yeshua through her testimony. By contrast, some religious leaders who were deeply versed in Scripture possessed the Scriptures yet rejected the One to whom those Scriptures bore witness. This is the paradox of John 5:39-40. They search the Scriptures because they think they have eternal life in them, yet they refuse to come to Yeshua to receive life.
Chapter 11 The Greatest Stumbling Block Was the Cross

The claim that Yeshua was connected with God was already difficult to accept, but an even greater stumbling block remained. It was the cross. If Yeshua had performed astonishing signs and then simply ascended, it might have been easier to regard Him as divine. Instead, He was arrested, questioned, beaten, handed over to the Roman governor, crucified, and truly died.

From a human point of view, this could look like decisive evidence against everything Yeshua had claimed. If He is God, how can He die? If He is the Messiah, why is He executed by Rome? If He is the Savior of Israel, why does He not save Himself? It is historically and humanly understandable that people looking at the crucified Yeshua found it difficult to believe that He was God.

Yet the Gospel of John does not present the cross as the collapse of Yeshua's identity. As the narrative approaches the cross, the language of glory becomes more prominent. The event in which Yeshua is lifted up is connected with His glory. What appears to be defeat from a human perspective is presented as the point at which God's self-revelation reaches its climax.
The cross can therefore be read not as a simple denial of divinity, but as the revelation of God in a form radically different from human expectations.
Chapter 12 The Resurrection Reverses Every Judgment
If the story had ended at the cross, Yeshua's claims could have ended as the claims of a defeated man. The Gospel of John, however, does not end with the cross. It moves to the resurrection.
Thomas answered Yeshua, "My Lord and my God."

This confession connects the beginning and the end of the Gospel. John opens by declaring that the Word was God. In chapter 20, a human disciple stands before the risen Yeshua and addresses Him as his God.

The movement runs from the Word who was God in the beginning, to the Word made flesh, to rejection, death on the cross, resurrection, and finally the confession, "My Lord and my God." The resurrection is therefore not merely one more miracle. It becomes the event that compels a final re-evaluation of everything Yeshua had said about His own identity.
Chapter 13 Do the Words "Father" and "Son" Mean Two Gods?
A necessary objection remains. If Yeshua is truly God, why does He continually speak about the Father, pray to the Father, and say that He was sent by the Father?

The Gospel of John itself does not allow the problem to be solved by saying that there is no distinction at all between the Father and the Son. John 1:1 says that the Word was with God and also that the Word was God. In John 17, Yeshua speaks of the glory He had with the Father before the creation of the world and of the love that existed before the world began.

The language of Father and Son therefore cannot easily be treated as something created only after the incarnation in Bethlehem. Yet it is equally inconsistent with John to divide the Father and the Son into two independent Gods. Yeshua says, "I and the Father are one." He says, "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father." He also says that He is in the Father and the Father is in Him.

John preserves both distinction and unity. Relational distinction exists, but the divine being is not divided into two gods. In the incarnation, Yeshua speaks and acts as a true human being. He obeys the Father, prays, is sent, and dies. At the same time, the same subject speaking through that humanity identifies His own existence as prior to Abraham, gives life, executes judgment, and says that to see Him is to see the Father.

The language of Father and Son is therefore better understood not as evidence for two Gods, but as language that reveals the relational manner in which God's self-revelation appears in the incarnation. This reading accounts for the full range of Johannine material more consistently.
Chapter 14 Conclusion
The question John leaves with the reader is ultimately this. If the God whom Israel sought through Scripture actually appeared before them as a human being, would they recognize Him?

John records that many did not. It was not simply because they were ignorant of Scripture. They studied Scripture, honored Moses, confessed the one God, rejected idols, and waited for the Messiah. Yet when God's actual self-revelation appeared in a form different from what they expected, their own certainty became a stumbling block.

To them, Yeshua was a man from Galilee. Yet Yeshua declared that He existed before Abraham. When asked to show the Father, He said that seeing Him was seeing the Father. When His hearers could not believe His words, He told them to judge by His works, and the signs testified to His claims. Even so, they judged Him as a man who made Himself God.

In the end, Yeshua died on the cross. At that moment, human judgment could seem to vindicate His opponents. The resurrection reversed that judgment, and the final confession before the risen Yeshua was, "My Lord and my God."

The argument of this essay can be compressed into one statement. It was not a man raising himself up to become God. It was God humbling Himself and coming as a man. The problem was not that God remained hidden. The problem was that He revealed Himself in a form so unmistakably human that many failed to recognize Him.

John does not describe that failure to recognize Him as a mere failure of perception. The true Light came into the world, yet the world did not know Him, and His own did not receive Him. John also says that the Light came into the world, but people loved darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil. The deepest reason they failed to recognize Him was therefore not only that His appearance differed from their expectations. The darkness was within us. That darkness kept us from recognizing the true Light, and that darkness was our sin.

Yet He came as the true Life and the true Light, full of grace and truth. John bears witness to Him as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and Yeshua says that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. The One whom our darkness kept us from recognizing accepted death on the cross in order to deal with the very sin that kept us in darkness. To ordinary human wisdom, the death of God at human hands appears incomprehensible and contradictory. In the movement of John's Gospel, however, the cross is the place where God's love and salvation are revealed most deeply. The deepest paradox of the incarnation and the cross is that the One who came as Light gave His own life to overcome the sin and darkness that human wisdom could not solve.

The God recorded by Moses, the God whose glory Isaiah saw, the God who existed before Abraham, the God who gives life and executes judgment, and the God who reveals the invisible Father draws near to humanity in Yeshua in the Gospel of John.

To believe in Yeshua in the Gospel of John therefore means more than acknowledging a great messianic figure. It means recognizing the God of Israel who has revealed Himself in this human being. That remains the most fundamental question John places before the reader, both then and now.
